diagrams.name: comm-p268-skew
diagrams.title: Positive and negative skew: where mean, median and mode fall

cloze.text: On the evidence pyramid, the top tiers — clinical practice guidelines and meta-analyses/systematic reviews — are {{c1::secondary, pre-appraised (filtered)}} evidence; RCTs, cohort and case-control studies are {{c2::primary studies}}.
Cohort and case-control studies are {{c1::observational}} studies; the RCT is the primary study that {{c2::tests a treatment}}.

Cohort studies are {{c1::prospective}} (an exposed cohort is observed for the outcome); case-control studies are {{c2::retrospective}} (subjects who already have the condition are studied, looking back for risk factors).

Below the primary studies on the evidence pyramid sit the 'no design' sources — case reports/series, narrative reviews, expert opinions and editorials — and at the very bottom {{c1::animal and laboratory studies}} (no humans involved).
cloze.extra: The book's table instead puts expert opinion lowest (below animal studies); the pyramid groups expert opinion with case reports. Both place these at the bottom of the hierarchy.

cloze.text: {{c1::Quantitative}} research = numbers, stats, measurable results (e.g., plaque scores, DMFT); {{c2::qualitative}} research = words, observations, patient experiences (e.g., case reports).
In a case-control study, a {{c1::case}} is a person with the disease or condition; a {{c2::control}} is a person without the disease, used for comparison.
The {{c1::independent}} variable is the one you change (the cause/intervention); the {{c2::dependent}} variable is the one you measure (the outcome/effect).
A {{c1::prospective}} study begins before the outcome happens and tracks forward in time; a {{c2::retrospective}} study looks backward — the outcome already happened and is traced back to exposures.
Purpose of PICO: to help form {{c1::focused clinical questions}} that guide literature searches and find the best evidence.
cloze.extra: Technique: break a clinical question into four parts to improve the clarity and precision of the search.

cloze.text: PICO: P = {{c1::Patient or Problem}}; I = {{c2::Intervention}}; C = {{c3::Comparison}}; O = {{c4::Outcome}}.
{{c1::Random}} sampling: every member of the population has an equal chance of being selected.
cloze.extra: Strength: reduces bias, best for generalizing. Limitation: can be time-consuming to set up.

cloze.text: Random sampling — strength: {{c1::reduces bias / best for generalizing}}; limitation: {{c2::can be time-consuming to set up}}.
{{c1::Stratified}} sampling: divide the population into subgroups, then randomly select from each.
Stratified sampling — strength: {{c1::ensures all subgroups are represented}}; limitation: {{c2::requires knowing subgroup info first}}.
{{c1::Systematic}} sampling: select every Nth person on a list.
Systematic sampling — strength: {{c1::simple to apply}}; limitation: {{c2::not truly random — hidden patterns may skew results}}.
{{c1::Convenience}} sampling: choose whoever is most easily available.
Convenience sampling — strength: {{c1::very fast and easy}}; limitation: {{c2::high risk of bias, often unrepresentative}}.
{{c1::Judgment}} sampling: the researcher picks participants based on familiarity or personal judgment.
cloze.extra: Strength: may be useful in special cases. Limitation: the MOST biased and subjective sampling method.

cloze.text: {{c1::Epidemiology}} is the study of disease prevalence in populations.
{{c1::Morbidity}} rate = % of people who got sick out of the total population at risk; {{c2::mortality}} rate = % of people who died out of the total population at risk.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: MorBidity — B as in Bed, sick but not dead. MorTality — T as in Tomb, death.

cloze.text: {{c1::Descriptive}} statistics describe data as-is (e.g., 'The average score of this class is 83%'); {{c2::inferential}} statistics use sample data to make predictions about a larger group (e.g., 'we estimate the district average is 83%').
The {{c1::mean}} is the average and is affected by outliers.
The {{c1::median}} is the middle number when scores are in order; the {{c2::mode}} is the most frequent score.
cloze.extra: WakeUpMemory: Median sounds like middle. Mode sounds like most.

cloze.text: A normal distribution is a {{c1::symmetrical (bell/Gaussian)}} curve in which {{c2::mean = median = mode}}.
In a {{c1::positive}} skew the tail goes right (low scores are more common) and mean > median > mode.
In a {{c1::negative}} skew the tail goes left (high scores are more common) and mean < median < mode.
{{c1::Standard deviation (SD)}} is a number that shows how far the typical score is from the mean (how much scores deviate); a larger SD = {{c2::wider spread}}.
Empirical rule: nearly all data in a {{c1::normal (Gaussian)}} distribution fall within {{c2::3}} standard deviations of the mean.
{{c1::Interexaminer}} reliability = consistency between different people; {{c2::intraexaminer}} reliability = the same person repeats it consistently.
Correlation is the {{c1::relationship}} between two variables, measured from {{c2::−1.0 to +1.0}}.
cloze.extra: The book prints '1.0 to +1.0' — a typo for −1.0.

cloze.text: The closer a correlation coefficient is to {{c1::1 (either +1 or −1)}}, the stronger the correlation — regardless of sign.
In a {{c1::positive}} correlation both variables move in the same direction (e.g., more sugar = more caries); +1 is a perfect positive, or {{c2::direct}}, relationship.
In a {{c1::negative}} correlation one variable goes up while the other goes down (e.g., more brushing = fewer caries); −1 is a perfect negative, or {{c2::indirect}}, relationship.
{{c1::No correlation}} means there is no predictable relationship at all between two variables.
The {{c1::p-value}} tells you whether results are likely due to chance; per the book, p = 0.05 means a {{c2::5%}} probability that the result occurred by random chance.
cloze.extra: E.g., p = 0.04 → a 4% chance the results happened by random luck.

cloze.text: A p-value does NOT tell you {{c1::how big or important the effect is}} — it only tells you whether it's likely real or due to chance.
p {{c1::≤ 0.05}} = statistically significant (the difference is real, not coincidence); p {{c2::> 0.05}} = not statistically significant (not enough evidence; cannot conclude).
A {{c1::hypothesis}} is a prediction made before starting a study.
The {{c1::null hypothesis (H₀)}} assumes no effect or difference; the {{c2::alternative hypothesis (H₁ or Ha)}} assumes there is a difference or effect.
{{c1::Statistical testing}} is used to decide if the results are strong enough to reject the null hypothesis.

basic.back: Combines data from multiple studies using statistical methods
basic.extra: TL;DR: strongest proof — top of the hierarchy. Example: a meta-analysis of 10 RCTs on fluoride varnish reducing caries in kids.

basic.back: Reviews and summarizes all high-quality studies on a topic
basic.extra: TL;DR: full-picture summary. Example: a systematic review comparing ultrasonic vs. hand scaling in periodontal therapy.

basic.back: Tests a treatment by randomly assigning people to an experimental or control group
basic.extra: TL;DR: fair test with real results. Prospective. Example: RCT on chlorhexidine rinse vs. placebo for gingivitis.

basic.back: Follows groups over time based on exposure to see who develops the outcome
basic.extra: TL;DR: watch what happens over time. Prospective, observational. Example: following students with and without bruxism to track TMD risk.

basic.back: Looks back to compare exposure in people with vs. without a condition
basic.extra: TL;DR: work backward to find patterns. Retrospective, observational. Example: patients with vs. without gingivitis — did flossing frequency differ?

basic.back: Studies one population at a single point in time
basic.extra: TL;DR: one-time snapshot. Example: survey on sugar intake vs. DMFT in teens.

basic.back: Detailed report on one or a few patients with unusual findings
basic.extra: TL;DR: first clue, not strong proof. Example: staining and taste changes after long-term chlorhexidine use.

basic.back: Tests effects in animals before human trials
basic.extra: TL;DR: not ready for human decisions. Example: a study in rats on enamel remineralization after fluoride exposure.

basic.back: Based on clinical experience, not original research
basic.extra: TL;DR: educated guess — lowest level. Example: the textbook recommends a brushing technique with no supporting study.

basic.back: Describes patterns — who, what, where, when — with no comparisons
Explains relationships — tests hypotheses and compares groups to find causes
Participants are randomly assigned to treatment or control — reduces bias
Groups are pre-determined — higher risk of bias/confounding
Neither the participant nor the examiner knows the group assignment
basic.extra: Best for avoiding bias.

basic.back: Only the participant doesn't know the group assignment (the examiner might still influence results)
Tries to test cause and effect WITHOUT random assignment
Includes randomization, control groups, and manipulated variables
A disease that occurs regularly in a specific area or population (= normal)
basic.extra: E.g., malaria in parts of Africa. WakeUpMemory: "Endemic ENDS as expected."

basic.back: A disease occurring in more cases than expected in a certain population (= spike)
basic.extra: E.g., flu outbreak in a school. WakeUpMemory: "Epidemic is an EPIC spike!"

basic.back: A disease that spreads across multiple countries or the world (= wide)
basic.extra: E.g., COVID-19 in 2020. WakeUpMemory: "Pandemic is Planet-wide."

basic.back: Number of NEW cases of a disease in a population during a specific time
basic.extra: E.g., 500 new flu cases reported in one month. WakeUpMemory: I for Incoming, I for Incidence = new cases showing up.

basic.back: Total number of EXISTING cases (new + old) in a population at a given time
basic.extra: E.g., 1 in 5 adults currently has high blood pressure. WakeUpMemory: P for Present, P for Prevalence = what's present, new and old.

basic.back: Results are consistent and reproducible
basic.extra: Reliability = consistency, not accuracy.

basic.back: The test measures what it's supposed to measure
basic.extra: E.g., if you're testing reading ability, does the test assess reading — not just memory or vocabulary?

basic.back: Whether the results of a study are trustworthy and free from bias within the study setting
basic.extra: E.g., a fluoride varnish trial controls age group, diet and brushing habits so differences in decay are truly due to the varnish.

basic.back: Whether study results can be generalized/applied to other populations or settings outside the study
basic.extra: E.g., a fluoride varnish study done only on teenagers in one city — do the results apply to adults or children in other regions?

basic.back: Ability to correctly identify those who HAVE the condition (true positives)
basic.extra: "If someone has the disease, will the test catch it?"

basic.back: Ability to correctly identify those who truly do NOT have the condition (true negatives)
basic.extra: "If the condition is not there, will the test say so?"

basic.front: People with more dental visits have fewer cavities. Does this prove visits cause fewer cavities?
basic.back: No — correlation is not causation (they may also have better home care or education). Experimental studies are needed to show causation.
basic.extra: Classic example: ice cream sales and drowning deaths both rise in summer.

basic.back: Compares the means (averages) of TWO groups to see if they are significantly different
basic.extra: E.g., comparing average brushing time between males (30 s) and females (45 s).

basic.back: Compares 3 OR MORE groups to see if at least one group's mean is significantly different
basic.extra: E.g., comparing average exam scores of students from four hygiene schools.

basic.back: Compares the frequency or proportion between categories
basic.extra: E.g., are men and women equally likely to prefer manual vs. electric toothbrushes?

basic.front: Two toothpaste brands are compared and p = 0.11. Interpret.
basic.back: 11% chance the difference in effectiveness happened by luck → p > 0.05, NOT statistically significant.

order.prompt: Rank these study designs from STRONGEST to weakest evidence.

mcq.question: A researcher identifies 50 patients with oral cancer and 50 without, then reviews their records to compare past tobacco use. Which study design is this?
mcq.explanation: Starting from people who already have vs. don't have the condition and looking BACK at exposures = case-control (retrospective). A cohort study starts from exposure and follows people FORWARD to see who develops the outcome.

mcq.question: Which type of evidence would provide the STRONGEST support for recommending fluoride varnish to prevent caries in children?
options: B. A meta-analysis of multiple RCTs
C. A cohort study of 5,000 children
mcq.answer: B. A meta-analysis of multiple RCTs
mcq.explanation: A meta-analysis statistically combines data from multiple studies and sits at the top of the hierarchy of primary/secondary evidence ('strongest proof'). One RCT is strong but below a meta-analysis of many RCTs.

mcq.question: A study tests whether chewing xylitol gum 3 times a day reduces Streptococcus mutans counts. What is the dependent variable?
mcq.explanation: The dependent variable is what you MEASURE (the outcome) — S. mutans counts. The gum (and how often it is chewed) is what the researcher changes: the independent variable.

mcq.question: Which design is BEST for avoiding bias when testing a new desensitizing toothpaste?
mcq.explanation: Random assignment reduces bias, and double-blinding (neither participant nor examiner knows the group) is best for avoiding bias. Single-blind still lets the examiner influence results.

mcq.question: A public health hygienist wants a sample of a school district that includes students from every grade, so she randomly selects 20 students from each grade. Which sampling method is this?
mcq.explanation: Dividing the population into subgroups (grades) and then randomly selecting from each = stratified sampling. Systematic sampling picks every Nth person from one list.

mcq.question: Which sampling method is considered the MOST biased and subjective?
mcq.explanation: In judgment sampling the researcher hand-picks participants based on familiarity or personal judgment — the most biased and subjective. Convenience sampling is also high-risk for bias, but the book ranks judgment as most biased.

mcq.question: A county health department reports that 1,200 adults currently have periodontitis, including 150 diagnosed this year. The figure of 1,200 represents the:
mcq.explanation: Prevalence = ALL existing cases (new + old) at a given time. The 150 new cases diagnosed this year would be the incidence.

mcq.question: On a board review exam, most students scored high but a few scored very low. The mean is 72, median 80, mode 85. How is this distribution described?
mcq.explanation: Tail to the left (a few low scores) with mean < median < mode = negative skew (high scores more common). Positive skew is the reverse: mean > median > mode, tail to the right.

mcq.question: Two hygienists score the same patient's gingivitis with the same index and both record 'moderate.' This demonstrates:
mcq.explanation: Agreement between DIFFERENT examiners = interexaminer reliability. Intraexaminer reliability is one examiner getting the same result on repeated measurements.

mcq.question: A new oral cancer screening device correctly identifies 95 of 100 patients who truly have lesions. This describes the device's:
mcq.explanation: Correctly catching those who HAVE the condition (true positives) = sensitivity. Specificity is correctly identifying those who do NOT have it (true negatives).

mcq.question: Which correlation coefficient indicates the STRONGEST relationship between two variables?
mcq.explanation: Strength depends on how close the value is to 1, regardless of sign: −0.85 is closest to ±1 (a strong negative correlation). 0.00 = no correlation.

mcq.question: A researcher compares mean plaque scores among patients using a manual brush, a sonic brush, and an oscillating-rotating brush. Which test is most appropriate?
mcq.explanation: Comparing the MEANS of 3 or more groups = ANOVA. A t-test compares only two group means; chi-square compares frequencies/proportions between categories.

mcq.question: A study tests whether a fluoride rinse reduces caries. H₀: the rinse has no effect. The analysis gives p = 0.02. What should the researcher conclude?
options: A. Accept the null hypothesis; the rinse has no effect
B. Reject the null hypothesis; the rinse likely helped
C. The result is not statistically significant
D. The rinse has a large, clinically important effect
mcq.answer: B. Reject the null hypothesis; the rinse likely helped
mcq.explanation: p = 0.02 is ≤ 0.05, so the result is statistically significant and H₀ is rejected — the rinse likely helped. The p-value does not tell you how BIG or important the effect is, so D overreaches.

mcq.question: What level of prevention is fluoride varnish application considered if the dental hygienist is using it when there are no carious lesions detected?
mcq.explanation: Primary prevention: fluoride varnish prevents the onset of dental caries by strengthening enamel and aiding remineralization. Primary prevention = stopping disease before it begins, avoiding the need for treatment altogether. (The book prints only options A–C; D was added for the 4-option format.)

mcq.question: What role does a dental hygienist take when organizing and coordinating an oral health program?
mcq.explanation: In public health, the administrator role involves managing, developing and coordinating oral health programs — e.g., planning community fluoride rinse programs, supervising staff, creating schedules, ensuring goals and budgets are met. Focused on logistics, organization and leadership rather than clinical care.

mcq.question: What is a limitation of school-based fluoridation programs?
options: B. Is not allowed in urban schools
C. Children are at school only part of the day
D. Uses rinse with too much fluoride
mcq.answer: C. Children are at school only part of the day
mcq.explanation: School-based fluoride programs can only be given during school hours, and school is not year-round. This intermittent exposure limits effectiveness compared with community water fluoridation, which offers constant access regardless of time or location.

mcq.question: What does incidence measure in epidemiology?
options: C. New cases over a while
mcq.answer: C. New cases over a while
mcq.explanation: Incidence = the number of NEW cases of a disease that occur within a specified time frame in a defined population; it shows how fast a disease is spreading. E.g., tracking 200 new flu cases in a city during January. Total cases (A) = prevalence.

mcq.question: What does reliability mean when referring to a dental index?
options: A. Measures what it's intended to
mcq.explanation: Reliability = consistent results regardless of when or by whom the measurement is taken. Intraexaminer: same examiner gets the same result multiple times; interexaminer: different examiners get consistent results with the same criteria. Reliability is about consistency, not accuracy — measuring what it's intended to (A) is validity.

mcq.question: A study finds a p-value of 0.04. What does this indicate?
options: B. Results are likely due to chance
mcq.explanation: Per the book: p = 0.04 means a 4% chance the results occurred by luck. A p-value of 0.05 or less indicates statistically significant results, and the null hypothesis is rejected.

mcq.question: If one variable increases while the other decreases, what type of correlation exists?
mcq.explanation: Negative correlation: one variable increases as the other decreases (e.g., as brushing frequency increases, plaque levels decrease). The relationship is inverse but predictable; the closer the coefficient is to −1.0, the stronger the negative relationship.

mcq.question: What does a high score on the Plaque Index indicate?
options: A. The patient has excellent oral hygiene
B. There is minimal plaque on all teeth
C. The patient has significant plaque accumulation
mcq.answer: C. The patient has significant plaque accumulation
mcq.explanation: On the Plaque Index a higher score = more plaque. The scale ranges from 0 (no plaque) to 3 (abundant plaque visible to the naked eye). A high score means poor plaque control and oral hygiene, requiring improved brushing and flossing.

mcq.question: Which index would be best to use for measuring the improvement of gingival health through some new education programs?
mcq.explanation: The GI measures gingival inflammation (color, swelling, bleeding). Gingivitis is reversible, so the index can monitor both severity and improvement; widely used in research and clinical practice to assess response to treatment.

mcq.question: What does the "d" in the deft index stand for?
mcq.explanation: The deft index measures caries in primary (deciduous) teeth: d = decayed, e = indicated for extraction, f = filled. It tracks visible decay experience in children, especially those younger than 6.

mcq.question: What is the primary focus of the Plaque Index (PI)?
options: C. Amount of plaque on specific teeth
mcq.answer: C. Amount of plaque on specific teeth
mcq.explanation: The Plaque Index (Silness and Löe) measures the thickness of plaque at the gingival margin on selected teeth, scored 0 (no plaque) to 3 (heavy accumulation). Used to evaluate oral hygiene status and plaque control over time.

mcq.question: Which is a cumulative and irreversible index?
mcq.explanation: DMFT (Decayed, Missing, Filled Teeth) is cumulative — it records past and present caries — and irreversible, because once a tooth is filled or extracted that cannot be undone. Commonly used in epidemiological studies of total caries experience.

mcq.question: Which term refers to the ongoing presence of a disease in a specific geographic area or population group?
mcq.explanation: Endemic: e.g., malaria in certain parts of Africa, or chickenpox in school-aged children (before widespread vaccination). These diseases are predictable and persistent in specific areas.

mcq.question: A patient learns that brushing twice a day prevents gum disease and begins to feel motivated to start. Which stage of the Learning Ladder are they in?
mcq.explanation: The patient now understands how brushing affects their health and begins to care personally about preventing gum disease. This shift from general awareness to personal relevance is the hallmark of self-interest.
